title: Conjoint analysis example: a worked study from design to output
summary: Follow a conjoint analysis example step by step, from choosing attributes and levels to reading the results, so you can create your own study with confidence.
body_markdown:
What are some conjoint analysis examples? +


Conjoint analysis is a survey-based statistical technique used in market research to show which features and price points consumers will trade off against each other. A smartphone manufacturer might test battery life against price to find the optimal product configuration for a new model. For a conjoint analysis marketing example, a brand could test which messages and offers to lead a campaign with, so its marketing strategy is based on consumer choice data. In a conjoint analysis survey example, each screen shows a few versions of the product side by side and asks which one the participant would buy.


How does the conjoint analysis calculation work? +


Conjoint analysis software turns the choices from data collection into utility scores, which show the relative value of each level. A level that participants chose more often, across all the combinations of other attributes, gets a higher score. To calculate an attribute’s relative importance, take the difference between its highest and lowest utility. Divide it by the total of those differences across all attributes, then multiply by 100. If price has a difference of 150 and the total is 410, price has a relative importance of about 37%. Running the survey results through a market simulator at different price points shows price sensitivity, which teams use to set pricing strategies and make strategic decisions about which specific features to include.


How do you turn a list of attributes into choice tasks? +


Conjoint software builds the tasks from your attributes and levels. Even a few attributes can make more possible products than anyone could compare. For example, five attributes with three levels each make 243 products. The software picks a balanced set and spreads it across the choice tasks. Using price points and features that exist in the market keeps each conjoint question a realistic trade-off, close to a real purchasing decision.


How should you design tasks for features other than price? +


Describe each level in specific terms participants can compare at a glance, such as “Next-day delivery” or “Up to 10 titles”. Keep the wording and format the same in every task, so any change in choice comes from the level itself. The same goes for claims and packaging: each level should be an option a consumer could buy.


When should you use CBC, ACBC or ACA? +


Choice-based conjoint analysis (CBC), also called discrete choice conjoint analysis, suits studies that test a small number of features on fixed packages. It’s also the easiest to explain to stakeholders, because every task looks like a real purchase. Adaptive choice-based conjoint (ACBC) builds each participant’s tasks from their earlier answers, so it suits studies with many features. Adaptive conjoint analysis (ACA) is an older conjoint method. It starts with self-explicated conjoint questions, where participants rate how important each feature is, then shows pairs of partial products. Sawtooth Software, which created ACA, now generally recommends CBC or ACBC instead.


How do you explain attributes, levels, profiles, and tasks to stakeholders? +


An attribute is a feature, such as video quality, and its levels are the options within it, such as HD or 4K. A profile is one complete product with a level for every attribute. A task is one screen where participants choose between a few profiles. The results show the relative value of each level, which is what stakeholders make decisions on.
